title: SFI26 Window 2: an update

content.content: Farmers have had a difficult 2026: navigating the impact of extreme drought and hot weather, the ongoing rise in Bluetongue virus cases, and input price rises from the Middle East conflict.

The exceptional demand for the Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) demonstrates farmers’ desire to invest in the environment, because healthy soils and thriving habitats are fundamental for farm profitability, productivity, sustainability & resilience.

In anticipation of high demand, Ministers decided to allocate an additional £20m to Window 2, on top of the £50m announced by the Prime Minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible.

We have therefore allocated a total of £310m to new agreements across both application windows in SFI26, £253m through Window 2. These agreements will invest a total of £930m in environmentally sustainable farming over the next 3 years.
This year we ensured small farms and those new to Environmental Land Management (ELM) revenue schemes were prioritised - with an exclusive first window earlier in the summer.

Previously a quarter of SFI funding headed to just 4% of farms making claims. That is why we capped SFI26 agreements at £100,000 per year. We also reduced some payment rates for a number of actions in order to ensure the available budget could stretch further.
Still, we know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be disappointed not to have secured an agreement this year.

In keeping with the commitments made in the Farming Roadmap 2050, we plan to offer an SFI scheme in 2027. We will look to open the 2027 offer as early as possible to ensure farmers can access funding.

We are ready to look at how we can improve SFI for next year – continuing our close work with farmers and stakeholders by listening to experiences and learning lessons from this window. As part of this, we are exploring alternatives to a first come, first served application process for SFI in 2027.

Farmers can still apply for Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) funding via the Expression of Interest (EOI) process. You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.
Next steps for SFI26

The RPA is working through queries from farmers and agents received via email as quickly as possible They have already returned calls for anyone who rang yesterday before Window 2 closed for applications.
Now Window 2 has closed, the Rural Payments Agency (RPA) will process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible.

As a reminder, if you started an application but did not submit it before Window 2 closed, you will not be able to submit it. This is because we closed the window when we had enough applications to allocate the full Window 2 budget.
We will allow two small ‘exception groups’, who contacted the RPA before Window 2 closed, to continue with their applications. They are:

The RPA will contact ‘started but not submitted’ Window 2 farmers in due course to confirm whether their applications will be withdrawn, or if they’re in an exception group and can continue with their application.
Applications are processed in the order in which they were submitted. Some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to assess.
We will provide an update on when successful applicants can expect to receive their agreement offer in due course.
SFI26 Window 2 statistics at a glance
We are conducting a final analysis of Window 2 application statistics. We will publish an official statistics release at 9:30am on Friday 25 September.
Numbers have been rounded to help illustrate the overall picture and should be treated as indicative rather than exact.

These figures are based on the applications we received at the point we closed Window 2 for applications, and the information provided by applicants at the point of application. They do not reflect final agreement figures, as applications are still being processed and the RPA handles farmers in the exception groups. As a result, final contracted uptake, including the actions selected, areas covered and associated values, may differ from these initial figures.
Applications
Approximately 12,200 applications were submitted during Window 2. Against our budget of £253 million, this means the average agreement value applied for was approximately £20,700.

More than 8,800 of those farmers have an ELM revenue agreement expiring on or before 28 February 2027. The new functionality in the SFI26 application service allowed farmers to start an application early for the full range of available SFI26 actions on land in an existing ELM revenue agreement before that agreement ends. Previously, these farmers would have had to wait until their existing agreement ended before being able to do this.
Over 1,100 farmers who applied in Window 2 are farmers who don’t have an existing ELM revenue agreement.
Top 5 actions
Applicants selected actions across all 14 SFI26 action groups, reflecting the flexibility of the scheme and the diversity of farming businesses taking part. The most popular actions were:
CLIG3: Manage grassland with very low nutrient inputs – over 7,400 applications

The benefits of this action extend beyond biodiversity. When established alongside cropped land, species-rich grasslands can support the natural processes that underpin resilient food production. Flower-rich habitats provide resources for pollinators and other beneficial insects, while diverse vegetation offers shelter for species that contribute to natural pest regulation. These areas can also slow surface water movement, reducing soil and nutrient losses and helping to retain valuable resources within the farmed landscape.
CHRW2: Manage hedgerows – over 4,300 applications

Well-managed hedgerows can support the natural processes that contribute to resilient food production. Flowering hedgerows provide resources for pollinating insects, while their shelter and habitat benefits encourage populations of beneficial invertebrates that can contribute to natural pest regulation and integrated pest management. Hedgerows can also help reduce wind erosion, slow surface water movement and improve the retention of soil and nutrients within the farmed landscape.
CSAM3: Herbal leys – over 3,300 applications
This action aims to maintain an established herbal ley containing a diverse mixture of grasses, legumes, herbs and wildflowers that provide varied root structures throughout the soil profile.

The ley should include areas of flowering plants from late spring through the summer months, supporting biodiversity and providing valuable resources for pollinators and other wildlife. The purpose of this mixture is to produce a high volume of forage while minimising the need for inorganic fertilisers, improving resilience to drought, and helping to enhance and maintain the soil’s structure, carbon content, biological activity and overall fertility.
CAHL2: Winter bird food on arable and horticultural land – over 2,600 applications

This action supports the growth of a mix of seed-bearing crops that supply vital small seeds from late autumn through late winter for species like finches, buntings, sparrows, and partridges. The seed mix also encourages summer flowering plants that provide nectar and pollen for beneficial insects, including bumblebees, solitary bees, butterflies, and hoverflies. It also supports natural predators of crop pests through an integrated pest management (IPM) approach when strips or blocks are planted close to cropped areas.
CIPM4: No use of insecticide on arable crops and permanent crops – over 2,600 applications

By encouraging no insecticide usage, this SFI action protects beneficial insects like bees, butterflies, and natural pest predators, stops chemical residues from running off into nearby streams, rivers, and groundwater or drifting into the air.

title: Sewage detectives: how UKHSA is using wastewater to track common viruses and emerging threats

content.content: The wastewater that we send from our toilets towards sewage treatment plants every day is potentially rich in data about our health. For the past 4 years, UKHSA has been monitoring wastewater across England for signs of polio, and over the past year has been testing new technologies to detect other potential threats. The next phase of the programme – made possible by a £3 million investment from the UK Integrated Security Fund (ISF) - will expand our capabilities and enable us to publish new data.
What is PRISM, and why does it matter?

Pathogen Risk Intelligence through Surveillance and Modelling (PRISM) is UKHSA's expanding wastewater and environmental surveillance programme, designed to detect a wide range of pathogens that could affect public health.

What makes PRISM different from traditional wastewater surveillance is that it isn't limited to a single pathogen. Instead, one sample of wastewater can be tested for many different threats at once. This gives significantly more value from every sample collected.
What has the programme achieved over the past year?

The team's biggest achievement has been proving this multi-pathogen approach actually works. Before PRISM, wastewater testing in government tended to focus on one target at a time. Now, UKHSA has demonstrated that a single sample can support public health surveillance, biosecurity monitoring and tracking of antimicrobial resistance simultaneously.

This proof of concept has opened doors that were previously closed. UKHSA is now working with government and academic partners to realise the vision of ‘sample once – test many’. Exploring how wastewater surveillance could support their specific needs, from targeted testing to detecting diseases arising from interactions between humans, animals and the environment.

The programme's surveillance network currently covers the wastewater of around 25 million people across England, a scale made possible by building on infrastructure already in place for the UK's polio elimination programme.
What is currently being monitored?

Right now, PRISM is testing for a range of pathogens including norovirus, enterovirus, flu A, flu B, rhinovirus, RSV and COVID-19 identifiers. The current approach detects presence or absence, rather than tracking trends over time. In parallel, PRISM is also taking a less targeted approach that can detect any or all pathogens in a sample without needing to know beforehand what specific organism is present. This is vital if we are to better detect new or unusual pathogens.

One area where PRISM is already delivering practical value is norovirus, the winter vomiting bug. The programme can track norovirus strains circulating across the country, helping build a clearer picture of the pressures facing the NHS each winter.
What's changing in the coming year?

New investment is enabling the programme to build new technology-driven capabilities, allowing for PRISM to unlock more value from wastewater. We are adding new sites, increasing our coverage and improving our ability to detect pathogens that were previously hard to detect. The programme - through new automation technologies - is now better able to scale to demands and make these new approaches more accessible to others. A key outcome for the programme, is bridging the gap between data and action. Using these new technologies, and data analytics, we can now build a system that goes from sample, to data, to insight and action.
Before this data is used more widely, it will be tested and compared against other technologies to check its reliability and accuracy, since different pathogens behave differently in wastewater.
What new pathogens will PRISM look for?

The programme has confirmed a set of new targets to prioritise for the coming year, taking advantage of one of our capabilities, chosen to reflect the range of threats the team wants to be ready for. These include diseases with existing elimination goals, such as mpox and measles, alongside emerging threats like avian influenza, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, West Nile virus, Lassa fever and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV).

The list also includes hepatitis A and hepatitis E, and 2 priorities in the fight against antimicrobial resistance: Candidozyma auris and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae, both of increasing concern to public health experts worldwide.
These targets have been selected to strengthen preparedness and support earlier detection of potential public health threats, rather than because they are currently widespread in the UK.
Building the capability to detect these targets earlier means the country will be better prepared for emerging threats.
What does the future hold?

Beyond new pathogens, over the coming year PRISM will explore targeted surveillance in new environments such as targeted hospital wastewater sites and high-footfall locations, including transport hubs, alongside exploratory work on air surveillance. This work will help assess where environmental surveillance could add most value.
The team is also exploring how this data could support hospitals directly, potentially helping to spot antimicrobial resistance outbreaks early and easing pressure on NHS beds.

Longer term, the ambition is for PRISM to become a permanent, business-as-usual capability within UKHSA, integrated with existing public health surveillance systems so that findings can directly inform decisions and protect communities across England.

title: A postcard from Darlington

content.content: As No10 North gathers momentum, I wanted to offer a perspective from the other side of the Pennines – the Darlington Economic Campus, or No11 North as the Chancellor recently put it.

HMT has traditionally been one of the most London-centric of government departments so the move over the last five years to have a fifth of our staff based in Darlington has been a big change. But when we began creating the Darlington Economic Campus (DEC) in 2021, we wanted to do more than just establish a new government office outside London. Instead we had a vision to work differently with the other departments based here and with our external partners in the region.

Since we launched, we have been co-located with eight other government departments and ALBs. We have deliberately organised ourselves as one campus rather than as a collection of separate organisations. We sit alongside one another, share events and communications, and bring together colleagues with different expertise to solve the country’s thorniest policy issues.

We have also forged new partnerships with local and regional government, local businesses and the third sector. Through initiatives like the Community Mission Challenge we have undertaken joint projects with Darlington Council; and every week we hold different events and workshops on key policy questions with external stakeholders.
Partnership is how we get better results

The way we work isn’t an accident. We work in partnership with other departments because the challenges we face do not fit neatly within departmental boundaries. Growth, skills, transport, housing… everything is connected. Bringing departments together helps us move beyond institutional silos and focus on the outcomes that matter.

Just as importantly, our strong external relationships with mayors, local authorities, universities and public service providers give our policy makers direct access to experience on the ground: what is working, where barriers remain, and how national decisions are felt in different communities.

We showed the difference this makes in the recent announcement that mayors would receive a share of income tax revenues. Thanks to our work in partnership with local stakeholders, we understand what will turn the dial for them in shifting power, funding and decision-making closer to their areas. As we work alongside No10 North and colleagues across the government on this agenda, these relationships will bear even more fruit.
Hearing different voices

For us at HM Treasury, one of the campus’s greatest strengths is the range of voices it has brought into the organisation. The vast majority of my colleagues in DEC have been recruited from the surrounding region, and most joined the civil service from other sectors having not worked in government before.

DEC provides an opportunity for people who previously wouldn’t have been able to work in policy roles in the civil service to do so. It brings in a much wider range of people, with different experiences and perspectives, to improve our advice to ministers and the services we provide the public and to make sure we better reflect the country we serve.

I often hear from colleagues who grew up in the North East that previously they thought they would have to move to London to work on the complex and cross-cutting issues that they do currently. And now that the campus has been established for a few years, we’re seeing that people can not only get a job where they are from thanks to DEC, they can build a career.

On the launch day of No 10 North, the Prime Minister addressed critics by saying, “it’s not just a new office”, and I agree. DEC - and No 10 North – may seem to the sceptical like surface level changes, but if we put the energy and commitment into building partnerships, empowering local colleagues, and getting everyone round the table, then we can change the way our country is wired.
So whether you call us the Darlington Economic Campus or No 11 North, what we do is the same: delivering the best advice and action for ministers and the country we serve.

title: Build once, benefit many: driving business case transformation across government, one (agile) step at a time
authors: Ellie Katona, Senior Interaction Designer, Digital Process Improvement team

content.content: A business case is a framework used by government to get approval to spend public money and ensure the delivery of public benefits. Our user research with people across several government departments showed that teams face similar challenges with business cases writing and approval. They are regarded as disproportionate, long-winded, unclear and difficult to both write and approve. Each department is investing time and resources into solving these same problems.

We in the Digital Process Improvement team at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) like solving problems, and it doesn’t get more knotty than business cases (so far!). We’re a friendly bunch from across different backgrounds and disciplines, driven by a common goal of helping people do their jobs better, at MHCLG and across government.
Why reinvent the wheel when you can share the blueprint and the service? We have a huge opportunity here for proper, cross-government collaboration.
Sharing is caring

From the start of the project to improve the business case process, in partnership with our Approvals and Assurance team, our goal was to build something based on our guiding principles of putting people first, joining the dots and understanding data. Something robust, that could be 'plug and play' for any department who wanted help with their business case process.

We started with the triage service: a way for people to self-serve business case templates and guidance. People struggle to find the correct template, understand approvals and who to speak to, according to our discovery insights. In triage, people answer a few questions to find the template they need. They are also encouraged to partner with Finance and Commercial early on, fostering the idea that collaboration is key to a successful business case.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) showed an interest in the work we were doing; there were many similarities with challenges but ultimately an appetite for change and exploration was welcome and we were able to share with policy and digital teams our triage service to 'steal with pride'.
What’s under the hood of the business case triage service?
Upshot

Sharing our journey so far with BIST has reinforced the value of collaboration across departments, particularly when tackling common challenges. By sharing approaches, lessons learned and reusable components, we can speed up delivery, focus resources where they add the greatest value and save time and money. Not just for MHCLG but across the entire government. Our work to transform the business case process continues as we build out the end-to-end service, and we’ll aim to share more about our progress. Who next? Arm's-length bodies? Let’s go!
Want your own triage service or want to learn more?
Get in touch! Find us at businesscaseproject@communities.gov.uk.

description: Business cases help government make decisions about spending public money and delivering public benefit. MHCLG’s Digital Process Improvement team is applying user-centred design to make the business case process simpler, reduce duplication and support better collaboration across government, starting with a reusable triage service.

title: Success builds on success for newts and developers

content.content: By Stephanie Bird-Halton, Director - National Delivery at Natural England

The 2025/26 Annual Monitoring Report for Natural England’s District Level Licensing (DLL) for great crested newts has just been published. This blog explores the successes so far and shows that the scheme is creating high quality habitat for great crested newts, while giving developers more certainty and speeding up planning decisions. Through the scheme more than 51,500 new homes and more than 15,000 hectares of developments have been enabled and over 4,747 compensation ponds created or restored. Overall, it proves that development and nature recovery can successfully work hand-in-hand.

In England great crested newts, known for their striking orange and black spotted bellies and the male's wavy crest along his back, are very important in our pond landscape. In the last century, though, there has been a sharp decline in the species mainly due to pond loss and intensive agriculture. Great crested newt populations are estimated to have declined by more than 40% since the start of the 20th century, while around two-thirds of ponds have been lost from our landscapes.

This has led to great crested newts being protected, with environmental regulations put in place to support their long-term future. To enable developers to more efficiently and effectively meet these regulations and to facilitate nature recovery across entire landscapes, District Level Licensing (DLL) for great crested newts was launched.

We have now published the 2025/26 Annual Monitoring Report for Natural England DLL and it demonstrates that the scheme continues to support nature recovery while giving developers greater certainty and helping local planning authorities (LPAs) progress planning applications more quickly.

DLL for great crested newts provides an alternative to the traditional sitebysite approach. Instead of surveying and protecting newts on site, developers can offset the evidence based predicted harm of their development by funding the creation of new ponds in places where newts are most likely to thrive, and the monitoring and maintenance of these for 25 years. This Annual Monitoring Report sets out the outcomes of Natural England's DLL scheme for 2025 to 2026 and highlights key achievements since launch. Its findings are consistent with the first five-year evaluation report, published in early 2026. For more information on these results read our blog post: The First Five-Year Evaluations of Strategic Licensing for Great Crested Newts.
High‑quality habitat for newts

By 31 July 2026 4,611 compensation ponds had been created or restored through DLL. That’s 967,000 square meters of pond habit, with terrestrial habitat made available to newts by the ponds. The Annual Monitoring Report showed that:

Great crested newts use networks of ponds and the expectation of DLL is not for all compensation ponds to be used by newts at the same time. Some scheme areas are less than five years old and ponds have fewer than five-years monitoring data. We look forward to seeing outcomes of the scheme as the survey data grows.
Habitat delivery partners recall success

Under DLL, developer compensation includes the monitoring and maintenance of ponds for 25 years by our Habitat Delivery Body partners, including Wildlife Trusts and Farming & Wildlife Advisory Groups (FWAGs). Ponds which are restored under DLL must be completely unsuitable for great crested newts in their current condition, meeting criteria to ensure additional habitat is delivered.

title: SFI26: Window 2 now closed

content.content: Window 2 of the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) closed at 15:48 on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Thank you to everyone who took the time to submit an application.
We have seen strong interest in the scheme and are grateful to all those who chose to apply in this window.
If you receive an agreement offer, please make sure you accept it within 30 calendar days, or the offer will be withdrawn.

If you are not successful in getting an agreement, eligible farmers and land managers will have another opportunity to apply for the SFI in 2027. We will publish details on next year’s SFI offer in due course.
Processing times

Now Window 2 has closed, the Rural Payments Agency (RPA) will continue to process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible. It’s important to note that agreements will only be offered to eligible applications if sufficient budget remains.
Applications are processed in the order in which they were submitted. Some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to assess.
We will provide an update on when successful applicants can expect to receive their agreement offer in due course.
Started but not submitted applications

If you started an application but did not submit it before Window 2 closed, you will not be able to submit it. This is because we closed the window when we had enough applications to allocate the full Window 2 budget.
We will allow two small ‘exception groups’, who contacted the RPA before Window 2 closed, to continue with their applications. They are:

The RPA will contact ‘started but not submitted’ Window 2 farmers in due course to confirm whether their applications will be withdrawn, or they’re in an exception group and can continue with their application.
Farmers who didn’t apply for Window 2 may be eligible to apply for the SFI offer in 2027. We will publish more details in due course.
Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs)
If you’ve applied for SFI26 on SSSI land, it’s important that you submit the required SSSI notice to get consent from Natural England as soon as possible.
The RPA cannot offer you an SFI26 agreement until you’ve done this.
Read section 10.1 ‘SSSI consent’ in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance to find out how to do this.
Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier
Other funding opportunities remain available.
Countryside Stewardship (CSHT) remains open to new applicants. Those invited to apply by Natural England can secure 10-year agreements, combining 132 land management actions and capital grant items.

Additionally, the new Expression of Interest (EOI) process provides a simpler route into CSHT. You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.
SFI26 statistics at a glance
We will publish official statistics on SFI26 Window 2 agreement and action uptake in due course.
Please subscribe to the Farming Blog to receive an email notification when we publish these statistics.
On 9 September, we published official statistics on SFI26 Window 1 agreement and action uptake.

These figures are based on the applications we received in Window 1, and the information provided by applicants at the point of application. They do not reflect final agreement figures, as applications are still being processed.
SFI in 2027
Ministers have committed publicly to stabilising the main design of SFI for the duration of this Parliament so that farmers and land managers know what to expect in the years ahead.
In keeping with the commitments made in the Farming Roadmap 2050, we plan to offer an SFI scheme in 2027.

Following Window 2 of SFI26, we will work with farming representative organisations and the wider sector to consider how we refine the scheme ahead of SFI opening in 2027. We will share more details as early as possible.

title: Hobbit Day and the legacy of Middle-earth

content.content: September 22 marks the autumn equinox and for me, without fail, the start of my annual Gilmore Girls rewatch. However, this year Stars Hollow is not my first stop. I’ve decided to go down a very different road, “and the road goes ever and on”, for September 22 is Hobbit Day!
A tale of two birthdays

This date wasn't chosen at random either. September 22 is widely celebrated as the shared birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins and was officially designated as Hobbit Day by the American Tolkien Society in 1978 as part of Tolkien Week.
Shall we go on an adventure

While Bilbo Baggins would probably have been happiest enjoying a quiet life in the Shire with a well-stocked pantry and no unexpected visitors, the world he helped inspire has become anything but quiet.

Nearly 90 years after The Hobbit was first published, Middle-earth, the fictional world created by Tolkien, has grown into a global phenomenon. Spanning films, games, merchandise, tourism and countless licensed products, this makes it one of the most successful examples of creative intellectual property ever created.
But let's start at the beginning...

In 1937, J.R.R. Tolkien introduced readers to Bilbo Baggins, a comfort-loving hobbit whose quiet existence is interrupted by an unexpected visit from the wizard Gandalf. Before long, Bilbo finds himself swept into an epic adventure, travelling far beyond the Shire on a journey of a lifetime.
The Hobbit may have started as a story told to Tolkien's children, but like many original creative works, it also concerns intellectual property.

Copyright protects original literary works, including books, stories, poems and illustrations . In Tolkien's case, that protection has helped preserve the unique world of Middle-earth and enabled rights holders to license and commercialise it in a variety of ways over the years.

Copyright helps ensure that creators and rights holders can benefit from the value of their work. In Tolkien's case, a story first published in 1937 has continued to generate cultural and commercial value for decades, long after Bilbo first stepped outside his front door. Tolkien died in 1973, so copyright in his works lasts until 2043, 70 years after his death.
An unexpected IP journey
Copyright may have helped protect Tolkien's original stories and characters, but it has also helped Middle-earth travel far beyond the pages of a book.

Through licensing agreements, Tolkien's world has been adapted into films, video games, music, merchandise and tourism experiences enjoyed by fans across the globe. If you’ve sipped a robust black tea from a Hobbit mug or wiped your feet on a Lord of the Rings door mat after an eventful morning hob knobbing around the shire, you’ve experienced the impact of licensing in action.
Nearly a century after it was first published, appreciation for The Hobbit shows no sign of relenting, proving that a great idea can travel far when protected through intellectual property.
Not bad for a Hobbit who never wanted an adventure in the first place.

description: J.R.R. Tolkien's stories have captivated readers for generations, turning Middle-earth into one of literature's most enduring worlds. This Hobbit Day, we explore the lasting legacy of Tolkien's work and the impact it continues to have around the world.

title: Supporting vulnerable people in the criminal courts: where we are now
authors: Melissa OGorman, Senior External Communications and Engagement Manager

content.content: Behind every case that comes through our criminal courts is a person. They could be a witness who must relive a frightening experience to give their evidence. Sometimes it's a member of the public serving on a jury. And sometimes it's someone who, for reasons of disability or vulnerability, needs the system to adapt a little so that they can take part fully and fairly.

Making this possible is something we care deeply about. In this blog, we explore the real, practical progress made this year: making better use of technology to support vulnerable witnesses, assisting deaf jurors, and making a small change of phrase that's made a big difference to some court users.
Section 28: pre-recorded evidence for vulnerable witnesses

For a vulnerable witness, giving evidence in a criminal trial can be daunting, particularly in cases involving serious or sexual offences. The Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999 allows witnesses to use special measures to give their evidence, with judicial approval. Evidence can be given in court from behind a screen, using a link into the court or in private.

Evidence can also be recorded and then played back in court. One of the most significant advances in recent years has been the move to an in-house system for recording evidence. Previously delivered through an external provider, the digital Pre-Recorded Evidence (PRE) platform means vulnerable witnesses can have their cross-examination captured in advance of the trial vat witness suits or at specialist locations they may already be familiar with, such as Sexual Assault Referral Centres (SARCs).

The service also now supports recordings from abroad, where a judge authorises it. We've already used this to record evidence from a child in America and a witness in New Zealand, meaning neither needed to travel or wait until they were next in the UK. Capturing evidence while it's still fresh also improves its quality.

This support extends to people facing serious ill health, where bespoke remote recordings can be arranged to allow them to give evidence in places such as care settings.  For witnesses who are terminally ill or living with conditions such as Alzheimer's, this flexibility can be vital, as waiting for a court date could affect the quality of their evidence, or their ability to give it at all.

The latest available statistics show that in 2024, more than 2,200 witnesses pre-recorded their evidence, sparing them the potential distress of attending court and being in the same room as the suspect.
Deaf jurors: a growing number supported through jury service

Jury service is a civic duty that shouldn't be closed off to anyone because of their hearing. Following changes to the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act, British Sign Language (BSL) interpreters can now enter the jury deliberation room, allowing deaf jurors who use BSL to serve in the same way as anyone else.
Since that change came into effect in June 2022, 110 deaf jurors have been supported by BSL interpreters.

For those individuals, this change means being able to fulfil a civic responsibility that had previously been out of reach. It also matters for the justice system as a whole: a jury that excludes people because of how they communicate is a less representative one, and every deaf juror who takes part strengthens the principle that justice should be accessible to everyone.

This also shows how legislative change and practical delivery work together. The law created the opportunity, but making it real has depended on getting the details right, from courtroom layout to how interpreters and jurors work together during deliberations.
"All rise, if able": a small change with a big impact
In May 2025, HMCTS changed one of the most recognisable phrases in the English legal system: "all rise" became "all rise, if able."

The change came about after two cases in the Court of Appeal Civil Division, where the adapted phrase was used to accommodate disabled court users present in the room. On both occasions, the modified phrase was warmly received, prompting us to roll it out across all courts and tribunals, regardless of whether someone with a visible disability is in the room that day. This phrase is being heard more frequently in our courts, boosting inclusivity and helping to ensure that more users than ever before feel represented.
Our Annual Report sets out the wider work we are doing to support court users who may need additional help, including those who require a sunflower lanyard for hidden disabilities.
Find out more
There is more to be done to keep improving accessibility across courts and tribunals and this remains a firm commitment.
To find out more about the work we are doing in this area, you can listen to our podcast. You can also read our blog on supporting deaf jurors.

title: Bringing Clean Power and Nature Together

content.content: By Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England

In this blog, Natural England’s chair reflects on a recent site visit to a Suffolk port, from where he sailed out to see an offshore wind farm as well as a novel installation to help one of the North Sea’s iconic species.  Here where industry and wildlife must coexist in a rapidly changing environment, positive opportunities for nature can still be achieved alongside achieving UK energy security, provided regulators and developers work closely together towards a mutual goal of ‘low carbon, high nature’ development.

The North Sea is one of the busiest and most pressured areas of ocean in the world. Surrounded by a number of developed countries it has for centuries been subject to fishing pressures, the effects of land-based pollution, infrastructure development and now climate change.

The flip side of those pressures are a series of benefits which have sustained many of England’s communities for a correspondingly long time, ranging from trade, food, construction materials and energy supplies. In modern times the big question is how to sustain that flow of benefits while protecting and restoring the health of that marine system, including its huge range of coastal and marine wildlife. Key to finding answers is good planning and collaborative working, and not least in relation to fast-growing demand for clean electricity.

The UK is now embarked on a clean power revolution. It needs to move at speed and at scale, so that we can play our part in getting to zero carbon emissions by mid-century, and ideally sooner if we possibly can. This is going to require investment, infrastructure, skills, complex supply chains, logistics and joined-up delivery.

Nowhere is this combination more evident than at the port like Lowestoft. Recently a declining fishing port town on the Suffolk coast, it is now at the forefront of the offshore energy revolution. The port itself, owned by Associated British Ports (ABP), has recently expanded with the £35 million of investment to create the Eastern Energy Facility (LEEF): an increasingly vital hub for enabling both the construction and ongoing maintenance of offshore windfarms, such as the four East Anglia installations in operation or under construction by ScottishPower Renewables (SPR).

Natural England is working with these developers and many others to help ensure that infrastructure such as new port developments and offshore windfarms can progress, generating with it local jobs and opportunity, whilst at the same time protecting wildlife while giving the space it needs to adapt to in a fast-changing world.

Offshore wind is an absolutely critical component of the Government's aim to decarbonise the energy sector by 2030. This forms part of the Government's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan which recognises the need to integrate clean power and the natural environment to tackle the climate and Nature crises. Similarly, in Natural England’s new  Strategy, we set out how recovering Nature will be a vital pillar to help deliver the infrastructure that the country needs - and that includes our precious marine environment.
Protecting marine life
I visited Lowestoft to hear directly from ABP and SPR about their work, and how we at Natural England can help them do it while looking after our precious marine environment.
Fraser Murdoch, Head of Consent Compliance at ScottishPower Renewables, said:

As we headed out on a port pilot's vessel from the calm waters of the port into the choppier seas offshore, I thought about how challenging the construction of ever-larger windfarms - sometimes hundreds of square kilometres in size – must be. The scale of the engineering is mind-boggling, requiring purpose-built specialised ports to deliver turbine pieces, construction materials and personnel out to one of the hardest working environments on the earth.

Ports are recognised as a foundational industry and invest significantly to facilitate supporting the Government’s mission in making the UK a green energy superpower. LEEF provides exceptional demonstration of investment in state-of-the-art port infrastructure delivering deep water berths, operational storage space and additionally is future proofed to support alternative fuels and shore-power.
Supporting seabirds

As this complex logistical task has been planned, developers have also taken on the goals for the protection of the natural environment. One major challenge here, as it is elsewhere, is the impact on seabirds. Developers have invested with Natural England advice into a range of initiatives, including the removal of rodents from offshore islands that host seabird breeding colonies. By removing rats from these places, which take eggs and chicks of birds, some significant ecological benefit can be secured, helping to address potential impacts associated with offshore wind development. Another measure being deployed is the construction of artificial nesting structures.

The kittiwake is a graceful pelagic gull and is now a bird of global conservation concern, having experienced significant declines in recent decades. This species specialises in feeding on sand eels, a silvery shoaling fish that is struggling to survive in a warmer North Sea. Offshore windfarms are an important element of tackling those warming seas but also have the potential to result in impacts on kittiwake should birds collide with the turning blades. Ironically, some kittiwakes have found unlikely homes on oil and gas structures. As these ageing structures are decommissioned over the coming years, this means a potential shortage of nesting habitat for the species, putting pressure on other colonies.

This is where offshore wind developers such as SPR, RWE and Ørsted come in, all of whom have installed nesting structures on the quayside or a short distance offshore to provide additional nesting spaces. These may also reduce the pressure on coastal towns like Lowestoft, where, despite being loved by many residents, nesting kittiwakes are not always the easiest (or quietest!) of neighbours. It’s early days for these innovative schemes, but the nearshore structures installed by Ørsted have already attracted nesting pairs, and it was uplifting to see a few nests amongst the decoys placed to attract birds in.
Benj Sykes, UK Chair, Ørsted, said:
Those first pairs and their young may be far out in the north Atlantic by now, facing even more challenging conditions than those faced by developers.

In parallel with this step, Natural England's advice has separately led to the closure of the North Sea sand eel fishery. This will be of great importance to birds - including kittiwakes, puffins, guillemots and gannets - while also helping the recovery of commercial fish species, such as cod and whiting, which also eat them.
Nature recovery

Returning to port, I mused on the progress being made but also the considerable challenges that remain in managing the vast but increasingly busy marine environment to ensure its benefits continue to flow. As our demands on the sea space increases, there is a pressing need for spatial planning in the marine environment that brings interested parties and the latest environmental evidence together to make the complex decisions about what should go where, and which activities are compatible with each other – including nature recovery. To assist those conversations, Natural England’s ground-breaking Poseidon project is generating the evidence needed to help identify the least environmentally sensitive locations for offshore windfarms, factoring in our seabed habitats, marine mammals as well as our seabird populations.
Collaboration is key

We are also working with Defra and other stakeholders to make it easier for developers to deliver environmental compensation measures for their unavoidable impacts, through the Marine Recovery Fund  which will deliver strategic, targeted environmental improvements on their behalf. We also hope our Rescue project will make a major contribution to reducing collision impacts by developing a more precise understanding of seabird flight heights, reducing the need for compensation in the first place. Industry is already innovating by engineering structures with blades higher off the sea surface, and Natural England will be providing world-class scientific evidence to assist those designs.

All this activity is hard-wired into Natural England’s Approach to Offshore Wind, which we intend to update and improve in the coming months, to ensure we are doing as much as we can to help progress ‘low carbon, high nature’ developments.
Tim Morris, Group Head of Corporate Communications for Associated British Ports (ABP) said:

As I departed Lowestoft, I was reminded of the social context for all of this. This is England's most easterly town and has always relied on the sea for its economic wellbeing, yet during recent times has, like the huge fish stocks that once sustained it, been in decline. Today Lowestoft has high levels of social deprivation and is in urgent need of regeneration. The offshore wind industry and its associated port modernisation is an important source of that, already bringing billions of pounds of investment through the town, creating hundreds of good jobs and bringing indirect benefits via hotels, restaurants, pubs, taxis and more. It is this that drives our work at Natural England, seeking to recover Nature for growth, health and security.
There is still much for us all to do, but I left Lowestoft convinced that there was a sustainable future for the North Sea, its communities and wildlife, provided we work together to achieve it.

title: SFI26: Window 2 now open

content.content: Today we’re opening the second application window for the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) offer.
SFI26 Window 2 has a total budget of £233 million, which includes:

We are committed to being as transparent as possible as funding is allocated throughout Window 2. We will continue to keep farmers, land managers and stakeholders updated throughout the application window.

We intend to publish an update on the Farming Blog when 25%, 50% and 75% of the available Window 2 budget has been allocated, in the same way we did for SFI26 Window 1 and the 2026 Capital Grants offer.

The length of time Window 2 remains open will depend on demand. In line with SFI Window 1 and the Capital Grants offer, we expect strong demand initially when the scheme opens.

In this post we remind you of what to do before you apply and provide information for farmers with soon-to-expire Environmental Land Management (ELM) revenue agreements. We also set out what to do if you started an application in Window 1 but didn’t submit it before the window closed.
Applying in Window 2
Window 2 is open to farmers and land managers who, at the point they start an application:
You can find the full eligibility criteria for Window 2 in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance on GOV.UK.
Before farmers and land managers start their SFI26 application, please read section 7 ‘Get ready to apply’ in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance.
Started but not submitted applications
Window 1
Some farmers who were eligible to apply in Window 1 started an application but did not submit it before Window 1 closed.
We kept most of these Window 1 'started but not submitted' (SNS) applications on the system. Applicants are able to complete their applications now Window 2 is open.
The RPA has written to these applicants to explain their situation.
However, some farmers with a Window 1 SNS application will need to start a new application now that Window 2 has opened. This applies where RPA has had to withdraw the original application because:
RPA's communication to affected farmers has explained what they need to do and why a new application is required.
Window 2

Window 2 will close once all funding has been allocated. We will not be able to accept applications that have been started, but not submitted, by the time Window 2 closes as we'll have enough applications to allocate the full budget.
Farmers with expiring SFI23, CSMT, CSHT or HLS agreements
We’ve introduced new functionality in the SFI26 application service for Window 2 to help farmers and land managers with eligible ELM revenue agreements that expire on or before 28 February 2027.

This will allow these farmers and land managers to ‘apply early’ for the full range of available SFI26 actions on land in their existing ELM revenue agreement before that agreement ends. Usually, they would have to wait until their existing agreement ended before being able to do this.

Where possible, it will allow those using this functionality to be offered an SFI26 agreement and accept it before their existing ELM revenue agreement ends – with their SFI26 agreement starting after their relevant existing ELM revenue agreement ends.
This will give greater certainty to these farmers and land managers about the ongoing management of their land.

28 February 2027 is the latest date that would still give farmers enough time to apply for and enter an SFI26 agreement in this financial year. SFI26 agreements must start by 1 April 2027 to use this financial year’s budget. Farmers and land managers with ELM revenue agreements ending 1 March 2027 or later may be able to apply for future SFI offers.

You can find more information about the new functionality and how it works in section 3.8 ‘If your ELM revenue agreement is ending soon (Window 2 only)’ in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance on GOV.UK.
SFI in 2027
Ministers have committed publicly to stabilising the main design of SFI for the duration of this Parliament so that farmers and land managers know what to expect in the years ahead.
In keeping with the commitments made in the Farming Roadmap 2050, we plan to offer an SFI scheme in 2027.

Following Window 2 of SFI26, we will work with farming representative organisations and the wider sector to consider how we refine the scheme ahead of SFI opening in 2027. We will share further details as early as possible.
Learn more
Our ‘Get ready to apply’ guidance looks at what you need to do to prepare to submit your SFI26 application.
Video support
The RPA have made a step-by-step video that guides you through the application process, so you know exactly what to expect:
This week the RPA have published a new video that shows you how to fix ‘Land Use’ error messages for land parcels in your SFI26 application:
Please check that your digital maps show the correct details for any land parcels you want to include in your SFI26 application.
The RPA has created a series of how-to videos to help you update your digital maps:
AHDB's SFI cost benefit tool
The Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board’s (AHDB) SFI cost benefit tool enables farmers and land managers to calculate the financial benefit of SFI26 actions they are considering.
It will show you how much income you could receive from the SFI actions you want to apply for and the net income once the associated costs have been subtracted.
‘Getting started with SFI in 2026’  leaflet
Discover how SFI26 can support your farm and reward nature-friendly practices.
This leaflet provides an introduction to the scheme, including the actions you can take, the payments available, and the benefits for your business and the environment.
Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier
Other funding opportunities remain available.
Countryside Stewardship (CSHT) remains open to new applicants. Those invited to apply by Natural England can secure 10-year agreements, combining 132 land management actions and capital grant items.

Additionally, the new Expression of Interest (EOI) process provides a simpler route into CSHT. You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.

title: Every sample counts: working together to prevent Salmonella in UK poultry farms

content.content: In this blog, Stella Ntachampre, Veterinary Advisor at APHA, shares her perspective on the importance of protecting animal and public health, and the vital role collaboration plays in safeguarding the United Kingdom's food supply.

I grew up in a farming family. My grandparents kept livestock, including cattle, sheep, goats, and poultry. And long before I trained as a vet, I had learned something simple and profound: what happens on a farm never stays on a farm. Good hygiene, careful handling, and clean housing go on to shape the safety of the food we all eat.

That love of animals, and that instinct that farming done well matters to everyone, led me to what I do today: working for the ‘One Health’ team of the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA). APHA is a specialist government agency that is part of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), and it exists to protect animal and plant health to benefit people, the economy and the environment.

In my role, I have been involved in prevention and control of a range of diseases, both zoonotic (spread between humans and animals) and foodborne. I have carried out frontline work with farmers and others; and used surveillance, epidemiology (the study of how diseases spread and how to control or prevent them), and laboratory science to help manage disease risks.
This blog is a snapshot of why that work matters, and why it depends on all of us.
What I see every day

Over the years, I have come to appreciate how closely animal health, public health, and environmental health are interlinked. And nowhere is this truer than in the case of Salmonella. As a common foodborne illness, Salmonella can easily spread to people through consuming contaminated water or food, especially raw or undercooked meat, poultry, and eggs. Because of these risks, National Control Programmes (NCPs) were introduced by the government. They were developed in partnership with assurance schemes, farmers, the poultry industry, vets, scientists, public health and food standards specialists in local and central government. Their purpose is to help keep people safe. Crucially, these programmes mean working together to keep Salmonella out of the food chain.

My early lesson about the importance of working together is something I experience every day. I have learnt that food safety is not just a laboratory issue, or a farm issue, or a public health issue: it is all of them. It only works when every part of the system works together.
The egg crisis that changed everything

In 1988, in a TV interview, the Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Health, Edwina Currie, warned that “most of the egg production in this country … is now affected by Salmonella”. Egg sales fell sharply, and confidence in the poultry industry took years to recover. But out of that crisis came a determined, long-term effort to tackle Salmonella at source – on farms. Alongside industry assurance schemes and improvements in food safety practices, a more structured approach to controlling Salmonella developed over the following years. By 2007, formal NCPs had been introduced, making regular testing compulsory and setting out exactly what must happen if Salmonella is found. The aim was simple: stop the problem before it starts.
Why Salmonella still matters

Despite these efforts, Salmonella continues to be one of the most common causes of foodborne illness in the United Kingdom (UK). It can cause diarrhoea, vomiting, stomach cramps and high fever. In the young, elderly, and people with weakened immune systems, it can lead to hospitalisation or even death.

Salmonella cases in England reached a ten-year high in 2025 but the increase in human cases is not reflected in animal surveillance. This rise appears to be driven by multiple factors and, to date, there is no evidence linking this rise with UK poultry or eggs. Thanks to NCPs and farmers being vigilant and testing their flocks, and through DNA testing of the bacteria and tracing work, we can see that the UK’s on-farm controls continue to be very effective.
How we work with farmers to control Salmonella

The NCPs protect public health by reducing Salmonella across the commercial poultry (in this case chickens and turkeys) sectors, for example egg producers, breeding flocks and broilers. It relies on farmers/producers, vets, labs, public health, food standards, local authorities, working closely together.
In practice, this system works through four main steps:
Step 1 – keeping Salmonella out
On farms, keepers are responsible for ensuring clean housing, controlled access, safe feed and water, pest control and good hygiene practices. This we collectively call biosecurity.
Step 2 – regular testing of the flock for early detection of any problem

Farmers and keepers also have responsibility for ongoing sampling and testing for Salmonella. This involves a specific collection of samples from the birds’ environment, in line with a strict testing schedule. These are then tested according to internationally recognised standards at only approved laboratories.

Accurate sampling is essential because every sample contributes to our understanding of Salmonella risk across the poultry sector. By following agreed sampling procedures, producers help provide the reliable surveillance data that underpins the whole control programme. Where additional support is needed, APHA works alongside producers to ensure sampling is carried out consistently and effectively, helping to maintain confidence in the system and protect public health.
Independent assurance comes from APHA field staff and partners, who conduct official visits to verify compliance, biosecurity standards and sampling technique.
Step 3 – following the egg beyond the farm

Salmonella control does not end when birds leave the farm. APHA’s One Health work includes oversight of egg packing centres through Egg Marketing Inspectors. The food business operators also play a leading role in maintaining standards throughout the supply chain.
Step 4 – rapid response when Salmonella is found

When a regulated Salmonella strain is found, each case is investigated, working with the farmers to implement our statutory guidance. To protect public health, it may be required for farmers to restrict the movement of their affected flocks and eggs. While restrictions can be difficult for affected businesses, they are a key part of maintaining confidence in UK poultry products and preventing contaminated products entering the food chain. When this happens, we also coordinate with private vets, local authorities, food standards and public health teams. We know this has a significant financial and emotional impact on a farm, and we do our best to handle such situations as effectively and sensitively as possible to protect animal and public health.
What we have achieved – and why none of us can take our eyes off the ball

We believe that our work has made a difference. Since the NCPs were introduced in 2007, Salmonella levels in UK poultry have fallen significantly. According to APHA's 2025 annual report, the proportion of GB flocks testing positive for regulated Salmonella remained very low in 2025, at 0.43% in laying hens and 0.004% (<0.01%) in broilers, among the lowest rates in Europe.

However, there remains a risk of introduction of Salmonella to our poultry flocks from the environment, wild birds, rodents, and other breaches in biosecurity. Global trade brings new pressures: with recent incident investigations tracing human cases to imported eggs and poultry. Climate change is altering the habitats of wildlife that may carry Salmonella. And the poultry industry itself continues to evolve – larger farms, different housing systems, new production methods – all of which require the control programmes to keep pace.
A shared responsibility – from farms to homes

We have proven that this network of shared responsibility works. Farmers, assurance schemes, and processors invest in prevention; laboratories provide reliable and efficient testing; regulators ensure consistency and fairness; and animal and public health teams monitor trends. Together, we protect public health every day.
That commitment is what keeps British eggs and poultry among the safest in Europe. We firmly believe this is a status worth protecting.

description: Protecting public health starts on the farm. Discover how APHA, farmers, vets and scientists work together to prevent Salmonella, protect poultry health and keep food safe.

title: From catchment to coral reef: a new roadmap for cleaner coastal waters

content.content: A practical research roadmap for reducing land-based pollution and strengthening coral reef resilience
Michelle Devlin, Devin Rowell, Alexandra Steckbauer and Amelia Wenger,
Cefas, The University of Queensland, CORDAP, Wildlife Conservation Society, The Nature Conservancy

Improving coastal water quality is one of the most practical local actions available to help coral reefs cope with a changing climate. The new CORDAP roadmap asks where research and innovation can make the biggest difference. It also contributes to the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021–2030) through the Nutrient Pollution Global Action Network, an endorsed Ocean Decade programme.

Coral reefs support fisheries, tourism and coastal livelihoods, protect coastlines from storms and erosion, and have enormous ecological and cultural value. Yet they are increasingly under pressure. Climate change is the greatest long-term threat, while land-based pollution can make reefs less able to withstand and recover from bleaching, disease and other disturbances.

Wastewater from towns and settlements, nutrients and sediments from agricultural land, and pollution carried through rivers and groundwater can all reach coastal waters. Cleaner water cannot remove the threat from ocean warming, but it can improve the conditions in which reefs recover while also supporting public health, fisheries, recreation and coastal communities.
A catchment-to-reef problem

One of the central messages from the roadmap is that protecting coral reefs requires us to look beyond the reef itself. Pollution does not recognise the boundaries between farms, towns, rivers, estuaries and the sea. A nutrient applied to a field, sediment washed from exposed soil, or wastewater entering groundwater may travel many kilometres before reaching a reef.

Effective management therefore needs to follow the whole journey: where pollution comes from, how it moves, where sensitive ecosystems are exposed, what intervention can reduce that exposure, and how monitoring can tell us whether the intervention worked.
The roadmap follows five linked elements across the catchment to reef system.
Building the roadmap together

The roadmap grew from an international Water Quality Solutions for Coastal Habitats workshop held in Fiji in October 2025. Researchers, government representatives, practitioners, community organisations and technical specialists from across the world worked together to test assumptions, identify the most important evidence gaps and focus on research that could lead to practical implementation.

Priorities were assessed against feasibility, likely impact and cost-effectiveness, with additional consideration of scalability and equity. Three connected areas emerged for innovation and investment: (1) improving sanitation and reducing wastewater pollution, (2) connecting agriculture, catchment and reefs through integrated land-sea management, and (3) effective Nature-based Solutions to improve coral reef water quality.
Priority Area 1: Improved sanitation to reduce domestic wastewater pollution

Wastewater can carry nutrients, organic matter and disease-causing microorganisms into groundwater, rivers and coastal waters. In many reef regions, sanitation systems have been designed mainly around human health and service delivery, with less attention paid to protecting sensitive downstream ecosystems.

The roadmap calls for better tools to quantify how much wastewater pollution reaches the sea, identify which reefs are most exposed, and measure the ecological improvement that follows investment in better sanitation.
It also highlights the need for discharge standards and water-quality guidelines that reflect the sensitivity of receiving ecosystems, not just the performance of the treatment system itself.

These wider benefits matter. Better sanitation can reduce disease risk, improve coastal water quality, protect fisheries and recreation, increase water security, and ease pressure on reefs. Considering these benefits together can change how wastewater investment is valued.
Priority Area 2: Best practice management of agriculture and integrated land-sea systems

Agricultural pollution is often harder to manage because it is diffuse. Nutrients, pesticides and sediments can originate across large areas and move through many pathways. Storms can rapidly push pollutants downstream, groundwater can carry less visible pollution loads, and nutrients stored in soils and sediments may continue to affect water quality long after management changes.
The roadmap therefore emphasises pollution hotspot mapping, load apportionment and improved modelling to understand where, when and how pollution reaches reefs.
It also calls for practical trials of precision nutrient management, smarter irrigation, manure treatment, erosion control and other practices that reduce losses from farms.

The key test is not simply whether a practice reduces runoff at the farm boundary. It is whether that reduction can be connected to lower pollution loads downstream and, ultimately, to better conditions at the reef.
Priority Area 3: Effective Nature-based solutions to improve coral reef water quality

The third priority asks how natural systems can help. Wetlands, riparian vegetation, mangroves and other natural or restored ecosystems can intercept nutrients and sediments before they reach the sea. Living shorelines can reduce sediment resuspension, while carefully designed coastal systems may help treat pollution close to where it enters marine waters.

Nature-based solutions are attractive because they can deliver several benefits at once: cleaner water, habitat creation, carbon storage, biodiversity gains, coastal protection and greater climate resilience.

The roadmap calls for field trials that show what works, where it works, how systems perform during storms, what maintenance they need and whether reductions in pollution lead to measurable improvements in coral condition. It also highlights the need for reef-ready monitoring, reporting and verification so that benefits can be demonstrated consistently and compared across sites.
Monitoring the whole system

That connection requires monitoring from land to sea. Conventional sampling can increasingly be combined with low-cost sensors, satellites, drones and better data platforms. The aim is to link farm actions to catchment loads, reef exposure and ecological response, rather than creating separate datasets that never quite meet in the middle.

For reefs, monitoring therefore needs to combine water-quality measures such as nutrients, turbidity, suspended sediments and microbial contamination with ecological response, including algal cover, coral disease, recruitment and recovery following bleaching. New sensors, remote sensing and integrated data tools can help, but their value is greatest when they are designed around a clear management decision rather than simply generating more data.
From better monitoring to better decisions

A common thread runs through all three priorities: we need to become better at connecting action with outcome. A wetland may capture nutrients. A farmer may reduce fertiliser losses. A community may upgrade wastewater treatment. Those are important achievements, but the real management question is whether less pollution reaches coastal waters and whether the ecosystem responds.
Science is only part of the solution

One of the clearest lessons from developing the roadmap is that technology alone will not solve the problem. A technically excellent wastewater system achieves little if communities cannot afford to maintain it. An effective agricultural practice will have limited impact if farmers lack the support or incentives to adopt it. A successful Nature-based solution at one pilot site will not transform coastal water quality if there is no route to finance and scale it.

Policy, governance, finance, capacity and community involvement therefore sit alongside the scientific priorities. In many coral reef regions, particularly Small Island Developing States (SIDS), the challenge is not simply the absence of solutions. It is creating pathways that allow good ideas and successful pilots to become sustained programmes with the institutions, finance, skills and monitoring needed to last.

That also changes the way research should be designed. The roadmap places strong emphasis on co-design with communities, indigenous partners, governments, researchers, businesses and civil society. Bringing these perspectives together from the beginning makes it more likely that a solution will be technically effective, locally appropriate, affordable and maintainable.
A roadmap for action

Improving water quality cannot remove the threat from a warming ocean, but it can give reefs a better chance. Reducing sewage pollution, keeping nutrients and sediments on land where possible, restoring natural buffers, targeting interventions to the places that matter most, and improving the way we monitor the journey from catchment to coast are all actions that can be taken now.

The roadmap shifts the conversation from documenting pollution towards solving it. Its ambition is to strengthen the science behind water-quality decisions, generate practical and cost-effective interventions, improve coordination between research, policy and investment, deliver measurable reductions in pollution, and support the recovery and resilience of coral reefs and the communities that depend upon them. Through the United Nations (UN) Ocean Decade-endorsed Nutrient Pollution Global Action Network, the roadmap will also support the Ocean Decade’s ambition to deliver the science and solutions needed for a clean, healthy and resilient ocean.
Read the roadmap to find out more.
Healthy reefs begin long before we reach the coast and are built through collective action across the entire source-to-sea journey.

We gratefully acknowledge the contributions of all co-authors, reviewers, members of the organising committee, and workshop participants whose expertise, insights, and commitment helped shape the development of this roadmap and its research and development priorities. Their collective knowledge and experience were instrumental in ensuring that the roadmap reflects both scientific evidence and practical implementation needs across diverse coral reef and coastal management contexts

title: Tackling drought: why nature-based solutions are key to a resilient future

content.content: By Oliver Harmar, Natural England's Chief Strategy Officer

This blog explains how climate change is affecting England, with a focus on drought and wildfire, while suggesting the actions that we can take to restore the natural landscapes that protect us and increase our climate resilience.
Drought in England has of course always posed serious challenges for people and the natural world. What's changing is how often we face it.

This year alone the England will have experienced an exceptionally wet winter followed by a long, hot summer bringing about our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries.

As climate change makes droughts more frequent and severe, the question is no longer just how we respond to the crisis in the moment, but how we adapt for the longer term, as a society, to live in a more unpredictable climate.

It means building landscapes that are naturally more resilient, so they can withstand drought better, recover more quickly afterwards, and reduce the associated risks: wildfire, water shortages, crop loss and biodiversity decline. Nature itself holds many of the answers.
A growing and connected risk

Climate change is driving more frequent droughts and higher wildfire risk, with growing impacts on people, nature and water security. These are not separate challenges. Dry landscapes are fire-prone landscapes, and the two must increasingly be treated as connected risks, requiring cross-sector partnership working to support land managers on the ground.

The scale of what's at stake is significant. For example, In England, 65% of our drinking water comes from surface water such as lakes and rivers, much of it starting out in our upland areas. It means tackling the problem is priority work, for people and nature.
What we're seeing on the ground

Across our National Nature Reserves, drought is affecting water availability in ways that cascade through our landscapes and ecosystems. Ponds, rivers, dykes and wetlands have dried to exceptionally low levels. In some upland sites, species-rich environments have dried out completely, in some cases that may be unprecedented in our records. Lowland raised bogs have seen significant water table declines, particularly where they have not yet been restored, leading to peat breaking down when air reaches it and erosion.

Wildlife has felt these pressures acutely: breeding waders have struggled with reduced feeding opportunities and higher risk of chick dehydration, fish kills have occurred where oxygen levels have dropped, and some specialist wetland invertebrates, including white-faced darter and large heath butterfly populations, have suffered substantial declines.
And farmers are reporting significant reduced yields.

The overall picture is one of significant strain on landscapes that are already contending with multiple, sometimes conflicting, pressures. Some sites this year faced both unusually wet spring conditions and summer drought in the same season, a reminder of just how variable and challenging our climate is becoming.

Fires at sites like Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire illustrate the challenge starkly. Dried peat can burn for months, releasing stored carbon.  They are extremely difficult to extinguish once fire penetrates deep into the ground which also places pressure on our emergency services and people working on those sites to tackle.
Understanding the fuller picture

While the short-term impacts of drought are visible now, there are also impacts that emerge later and recur over time. Natural England is developing a research and monitoring programme specifically focused on the impacts of drought and wildfire, because many of the most serious consequences may not become fully apparent until future seasons.

We are also increasingly responding to drought permits and orders; requests to allow more flexibility in managing water resources when there is an exceptional shortage of rain. These measures are designed to avoid lasting damage, but they are growing in frequency.
Holding water for longer: restoring the systems that protect us
Restoring the natural systems that help our landscapes cope in the first place is critical.

In particular, restoring our wetlands and peatlands so they can do what they naturally would, is one of the most effective tools we have.  It helps them hold onto water for longer to reduce flooding and keep water where it should be helping them resist fire.  Wetter landscapes recover more quickly from drought and help maintain water levels for drinking water as well and water for our treasured wildlife.

Restoration of sphagnum moss on peatland is one of the most common methods.  Restoring this plant cover, alongside work like blocking artificial drainage channels, helps peatlands hold water much more effectively. Long-term restoration work in the Peak District and South Pennines, led by partners such as Moors for the Future, has shown that this kind of restoration can slow the flow of water off the hills, helping to protect communities downstream while also storing carbon and supporting biodiversity. It's a strong example of how work that's good for nature is good for people.

Beavers offer another compelling example. By building dams and creating wetlands, beavers naturally store water, filter it, and help keep the ground moist for much longer after rain has stopped, acting as both a lifeline during drought and a natural firebreak against wildfire.

Reintroducing beavers has real potential to support nature's recovery. Natural England is working closely with partners to manage reintroduction licences carefully, to make sure the return of beavers benefits both wildlife and local communities.
What this means for people
As hotter, drier summers become more common, climate-resilient landscapes play an increasingly important role in protecting people’s health and wellbeing.
Trees, parks, wetlands, rivers and other nature-rich spaces provide cooling shade, help reduce the impacts of heat stress, improve air quality and create places for recreation and relaxation.
As part of our natural health service, they help communities stay healthy, active and resilient in a changing climate.
Working together with the National Drought Group

No single organisation can tackle a challenge of this scale alone. Natural England sits on the National Drought Group. Working alongside government, water companies and other partners to coordinate our response to drought and ensure that the needs of nature are properly represented in national planning.

This collaboration allows us to bring our evidence and experience from reserves across the country into decisions that can improve water management, drought response and long-term resilience planning at a national level.
Looking ahead

On our National Nature Reserves, restored wetlands and bogs have consistently held onto water better than areas that haven't been restored, offering vital refuges for wildlife throughout drought periods. Habitats with more variety and structure, such as developing wooded areas, have proven more resilient than open, exposed habitats.

By continuing to invest in these nature-based solutions, deepening our research into the longer-term impacts of drought and wildfire, and working closely with partners through the National Drought Group and beyond, we can help build a landscape that is genuinely more resilient to the droughts of the future, for wildlife, and for the people who depend on it.
